concepts.name: Electric Charge
concepts.shortDescription: Fundamental physical property of matter carried by electrons and protons.
concepts.fullDescription: Matter consists of atoms with positive protons and negative electrons. The SI unit of electric charge is the Coulomb (C). 1 Coulomb equals the charge of approximately 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.

commonMisconceptions.title: Charge is Created by Batteries
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing batteries produce or create electric charges rather than driving pre-existing charges inside conducting wires.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Charge is conserved. Batteries provide the potential difference (work per unit charge) that moves charges already present in the metal conductor.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Static cling, electrostatic precipitators in factory chimneys, laser printers.

concepts.name: Electric Current
concepts.shortDescription: Rate of flow of electric charges through a conductor per unit time.
concepts.fullDescription: Electric current (I) is the quantity of electric charge passing through any cross-section of a conductor per second. Formally, I = Q / t. The SI unit is Ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C/s. Conventionally directed from positive to negative terminal, though electrons flow in the opposite direction. An ammeter is connected in series.

commonMisconceptions.title: Current is Consumed or Used Up
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing current leaving a bulb or resistor is less than the current entering it because electricity is "consumed".
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Current is the rate of charge flow and is conserved in a closed loop. The current entering a bulb is exactly equal to the current exiting it; electrical energy is converted to light/heat, but charge is never destroyed.

commonMisconceptions.title: Electrons Travel at the Speed of Light
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing electrons physically race at light speed through wires from the battery to the switch.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: The electric field propagates near light speed, setting all mobile electrons in motion almost instantaneously, but the electron drift velocity is typically only a few millimeters per second.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Household circuit breakers, charging smartphones, ammeters in testing equipment.

concepts.name: Potential Difference
concepts.shortDescription: Work done to move a unit positive charge from one point to another.
concepts.fullDescription: Electric potential difference (V) between two points is defined as the work done (W) in moving a unit positive charge (Q) from one point to the other. V = W / Q. The SI unit is Volt (V), where 1 V = 1 Joule / Coulomb. A voltmeter has very high resistance and is always connected in parallel across the two points.

commonMisconceptions.title: Voltage Flows Through Wires
commonMisconceptions.description: Saying "voltage flows" through the circuit like a liquid, confusing voltage with current.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Current flows through a circuit; voltage (potential difference) exists ACROSS two points or components, serving as the electrical pressure or driving push.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Battery ratings (1.5V AA cells, 12V car batteries, 220V household wall outlets).

concepts.name: Resistance & Factors Affecting It
concepts.shortDescription: The opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric charges.
concepts.fullDescription: Resistance (R) measures how strongly a component opposes current flow. It arises from collisions between moving electrons and vibrating metal lattice ions. R = ρ × (L / A), where ρ is electrical resistivity, L is length of conductor, and A is cross-sectional area. Resistance is directly proportional to length, inversely proportional to thickness, and increases with temperature for metals.

commonMisconceptions.title: Thicker Wires Have Higher Resistance
commonMisconceptions.description: Assuming a bigger or thicker wire has more "matter" to block electrons, so resistance increases.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Thicker wires have a larger cross-sectional area (A), offering more parallel paths for electron flow. Resistance is inversely proportional to area (R ∝ 1/A), so thicker wires have lower resistance.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Heating elements made of high-resistivity Nichrome wire, thick cables for heavy machinery.

concepts.name: Ohm's Law
concepts.shortDescription: Direct proportionality between potential difference and current at constant temperature.
concepts.fullDescription: Ohm's law states that the electric current (I) flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference (V) across its ends, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. V ∝ I, which yields V = I × R. The I-V graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line passing through the origin.

commonMisconceptions.title: Ohm’s Law Applies to All Devices Universally
commonMisconceptions.description: Assuming every electronic component maintains constant resistance under any condition.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Ohm's law applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature. Non-ohmic devices (like diode semiconductors or filament lamps whose temperature changes drastically) have non-linear I-V curves.

commonMisconceptions.title: Increasing Voltage Directly Increases Resistor Resistance
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing that because R = V/I, increasing V automatically increases R.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: For a fixed ohmic resistor, R is an inherent physical property determined by geometry and material. Increasing V causes I to increase proportionally, keeping the ratio V/I constant.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Dimmer switches, volume sliders, electronic circuit design.

concepts.name: Series Circuits
concepts.shortDescription: Single path for current; same current through all components, voltages divide.
concepts.fullDescription: In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end along a single path. Key characteristics: (1) Current I is identical through every component; (2) Total potential difference is the sum of individual voltage drops (V_total = V1 + V2 + ...); (3) Equivalent resistance is the sum of individual resistances (Req = R1 + R2 + ...); (4) If any single component is disconnected or burns out, the entire circuit is broken.

commonMisconceptions.title: The First Bulb in Series is Always Brighter Than the Second
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing that the bulb closest to the positive terminal receives more current than subsequent bulbs in series.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: In a series circuit, there is only one continuous loop. Charge cannot pile up or vanish. Current is strictly identical through every component in the series string (I1 = I2 = I_total).

commonMisconceptions.title: Removing One Component in Series Leaves Others Working
commonMisconceptions.description: Thinking other bulbs stay on when one bulb is unscrewed in a series string.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Breaking any point in a series circuit creates an open loop, dropping the current to zero throughout the whole circuit.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Decorative fairy lights (traditional), security interlock switches, fuse connected in series.

concepts.name: Parallel Circuits
concepts.shortDescription: Multiple branches; full voltage across each branch, currents divide.
concepts.fullDescription: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two common nodes. Key characteristics: (1) The potential difference (V) across each parallel branch is identical and equals the source voltage; (2) Total current is the sum of branch currents (I_total = I1 + I2 + ...); (3) Reciprocal of equivalent resistance equals the sum of reciprocals: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...; (4) Req is always smaller than the smallest individual branch resistance; (5) Each branch operates independently.

commonMisconceptions.title: Adding More Resistors in Parallel Increases Total Resistance
commonMisconceptions.description: Thinking that adding more resistive parts to a circuit must always increase overall resistance.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Adding parallel branches provides additional pathways for charges to flow. Total conductance increases, so overall equivalent resistance actually DECREASES. For identical resistors R in parallel, Req = R / n.

commonMisconceptions.title: Voltage Splits Among Parallel Branches
commonMisconceptions.description: Believing a 12V battery only gives 6V to each of two parallel branches.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: Each parallel branch is connected directly across the same two terminals of the battery, receiving the full 12V potential difference.

concepts.realWorldApplication: Domestic home wiring (appliances can be switched on/off independently and each gets 220V).

concepts.name: Electric Power & Joule's Heating
concepts.shortDescription: Rate of electrical energy consumption and heating effect produced by current.
concepts.fullDescription: Electric power (P) is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated. P = V × I. By applying Ohm's law, P = I² × R = V² / R. The SI unit is the Watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. Joule's law of heating states that heat produced in a resistor is H = I² × R × t. Commercial unit of electric energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules.

commonMisconceptions.title: Higher Resistance Always Gives Greater Power Dissipation
commonMisconceptions.description: Using P = I²R to conclude that high resistance always draws more power, ignoring how current changes with voltage.
commonMisconceptions.correctScientificPrinciple: If voltage is constant (e.g., household mains), P = V² / R. Therefore, a lower resistance component actually draws higher current and consumes MORE power. P = I²R only predicts higher power when current is held constant (as in series).

concepts.realWorldApplication: Electric irons, water geysers, electric kettles, incandescent bulbs vs energy-efficient LEDs.

questions.title: Charge in a Conductor
questions.questionText: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. What is the total amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit?
questions.expectedReasoning: Use Q = I × t. Convert time into seconds: t = 10 minutes × 60 s/min = 600 s. Then Q = 0.5 A × 600 s = 300 C.
questions.hint: Remember to convert minutes to seconds before multiplying by current.

questions.title: Current Conservation in a Lamp
questions.questionText: An ammeter placed before a glowing electric lamp reads 2.0 A. What will an ammeter placed immediately after the lamp read?

options.text: Less than 2.0 A, because current is consumed to produce light
Exactly 2.0 A, because charge is conserved in the circuit
More than 2.0 A, due to accumulated electron pressure
0 A, because the energy was completely spent in the filament

questions.expectedReasoning: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. Charges do not vanish or get consumed when passing through a resistor; electric potential energy is converted to light and heat, but charge is strictly conserved. Hence current in equals current out.

questions.title: Work Done Moving Charge
questions.questionText: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 Coulombs across two points having a potential difference of 12 V?
questions.expectedReasoning: Potential difference V = W / Q => W = V × Q. W = 12 V × 2 C = 24 Joules.
questions.hint: Recall the definition: V = W / Q.

questions.title: Effect of Doubling Conductor Thickness
questions.questionText: A metal wire of length L and resistance R is replaced by another wire of the same material and same length, but with twice the cross-sectional area (2A). What is the resistance of the new wire?

options.text: 4R
2R

questions.expectedReasoning: Resistance R = ρ × (L / A). Since resistance is inversely proportional to area (R ∝ 1/A), doubling the area halves the resistance: R_new = R / 2.

questions.title: Current Calculation with Ohm's Law
questions.questionText: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a fixed 4 Ω resistor. What is the electric current flowing through it?
questions.expectedReasoning: By Ohm's law, V = I × R => I = V / R = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A.
questions.hint: Use the formula I = V / R.

questions.title: Increasing Voltage on a Resistor
questions.questionText: If the potential difference across a constant ohmic resistor is tripled, what happens to the resistance of the resistor?

options.text: It triples, because R = V / I
It decreases to one-third
It remains unchanged, because resistance is an inherent physical property
It drops to zero

questions.expectedReasoning: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, resistance R is an inherent physical property determined by material, length, and cross-section. When voltage triples, current also triples, keeping the ratio V/I constant.

questions.title: Equivalent Resistance of Series Resistors
questions.questionText: Two resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in series to a battery. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
questions.expectedReasoning: In a series circuit, resistances add linearly: R_total = R1 + R2 = 2 Ω + 4 Ω = 6 Ω.

questions.title: Brightness in Series String
questions.questionText: Two identical 60 W bulbs, Bulb A and Bulb B, are connected in series across a 12 V battery, with Bulb A connected closer to the positive battery terminal. Which bulb shines brighter?

options.text: Bulb A, because it receives the electric current first
Bulb B, because negative charges flow towards it first
Both shine with equal brightness, because current is identical everywhere in series
Neither bulb will glow at all

questions.expectedReasoning: In a series circuit, there is only one pathway for current. The current flowing through Bulb A is identical to that flowing through Bulb B (I1 = I2). Since the bulbs have identical resistance, both dissipate the same power P = I²R and glow with equal brightness.

questions.title: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel
questions.questionText: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?

questions.title: Adding More Branches in Parallel
questions.questionText: A room has two identical bulbs connected in parallel to the mains. If a third identical bulb is switched on in parallel with them, what happens to the total resistance of the circuit?

options.text: Total resistance increases because more electrical devices are active
Total resistance decreases because an extra conductive path is added
Total resistance remains unchanged
Total resistance drops immediately to zero

questions.expectedReasoning: Connecting an additional branch in parallel provides an additional path for electric charge to flow, increasing total conductance and lowering the overall equivalent resistance of the circuit (1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3).

questions.title: Calculating Electrical Power
questions.questionText: An electric device is connected to a 12 V source and draws a current of 2 A. What is the power consumed by this device?
questions.expectedReasoning: Power P = V × I = 12 V × 2 A = 24 Watts.

questions.title: Bulb Rating & Resistance Dilemma
questions.questionText: Two bulbs marked "220 V, 100 W" and "220 V, 40 W" are compared. Which bulb has a higher electrical resistance in its filament?

options.text: The 100 W bulb, because higher wattage requires higher resistance
The 40 W bulb, because at constant voltage P = V² / R, so lower power corresponds to higher resistance
Both have identical resistance because they share the 220 V rating
Resistance cannot be determined without measuring current

questions.expectedReasoning: For appliances designed for the same voltage source (220 V), P = V² / R => R = V² / P. Resistance is inversely proportional to rated power. Therefore, the 40 W bulb has R = (220)² / 40 = 1210 Ω, while the 100 W bulb has R = (220)² / 100 = 484 Ω. The 40 W bulb has higher resistance.

questions.title: Three Resistors in Series
questions.questionText: Three resistors of 1 Ω, 2 Ω, and 3 Ω are combined in series. If this combination is connected to a 12 V battery with negligible internal resistance, what is the current in the circuit?
questions.expectedReasoning: R_total = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 Ω. Total current I = V / R_total = 12 V / 6 Ω = 2 A.
questions.hint: First find the total equivalent resistance, then apply Ohm’s law.

questions.title: Parallel Branch Current Ratio
questions.questionText: Two resistors of 10 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in parallel across a 20 V power supply. What is the current flowing specifically through the 10 Ω resistor?
questions.expectedReasoning: In parallel, each branch receives the full source voltage (20 V). Current through the 10 Ω branch is I1 = V / R1 = 20 V / 10 Ω = 2 A.
questions.hint: Each branch in parallel experiences the full source voltage.

questions.title: Voltage Drop in Series
questions.questionText: A 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are connected in series across a 24 V battery. What is the potential difference across the 8 Ω resistor?
questions.expectedReasoning: Total R = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. Current I = 24 / 12 = 2 A. Voltage across 8 Ω resistor V2 = I × R2 = 2 A × 8 Ω = 16 V.
questions.hint: Find the circuit current first, then calculate V = I × R for that specific resistor.

questions.title: Heat Produced in a Resistor
questions.questionText: A current of 2 A passes through a 5 Ω heating coil for 10 seconds. How much heat energy (in Joules) is generated?
questions.expectedReasoning: By Joule's law of heating, H = I² × R × t = (2 A)² × 5 Ω × 10 s = 4 × 5 × 10 = 200 Joules.
questions.hint: Recall Joule’s heating formula: H = I²Rt.

questions.title: Charges Flowing in Microamperes
questions.questionText: If 100 Coulombs of charge flow through an electronic component in 50 seconds, what is the magnitude of electric current in Amperes?

questions.title: Three Identical Resistors in Parallel
questions.questionText: Three identical resistors of 9 Ω each are connected in parallel. What is their combined equivalent resistance?
questions.expectedReasoning: For n identical resistors in parallel, Req = R / n = 9 Ω / 3 = 3 Ω.
